summary: A working draft of ANSI guidelines on how to structure the Domain Specific Part (DSP) of an ISO NSAP address. It advises private address administration authorities on preferred formats and meanings so that address assignment can be efficient. It is informational only and does not specify an ARPA-Internet standard.

eli5.summary: Addresses need a tidy pattern, like country, city, street, house. This memo gives advice to groups handing out addresses on how to arrange the last part of the address neatly.

questions: how is the domain specific part of an nsap address structured
what is the dsp in an nsap address
what fields are in a domain specific part
subtitle: A recipe for structuring the local part of ISO network addresses.

tldr.problem: As organizations deployed ISO systems across networks, they needed a standard way to structure the local portion of addresses (the Domain Specific Part) to ensure efficient assignment and interoperability between systems from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 982 provides guidelines for how the DSP should be divided into subnetwork identification, subnetwork address, and NSAP selector fields, with different recommended formats for addresses derived from different numbering authorities.
tldr.outcome: Organizations administering NSAP addresses can now follow a consistent structure, making it easier to hand out addresses and for heterogeneous systems to work together.

today: RFC 982 is an informational document and ANSI draft. NSAP addresses were designed for ISO systems, which competed with TCP/IP in the 1980s but never achieved widespread deployment. While the addressing structure the RFC describes is technically sound, IPv6 has since become the standard for next-generation network addressing.

sections.title: Addresses for ISO Networks
sections.content:
NSAP (Network Service Access Point) addresses identify services on ISO networks. Like postal addresses, they are hierarchical: each address is split into two parts. The Initial Domain Part (IDP) is standardized and identifies which authority is responsible for allocating the rest of the address. The Domain Specific Part (DSP) is what that authority gets to structure as it likes.

When organizations deploy heterogeneous systems—equipment from different vendors—each using its own DSP structure can cause interoperability problems. This memo provides guidelines for how to divide the DSP consistently across different numbering schemes, so a system from one vendor can understand addresses assigned by another.
sections.eli5: A postal address starts with a country code (standardized), then you can structure the rest however you want. But if everyone structures it differently, mail gets lost. This memo gives a standard way to organize the "local" part.

sections.title: The Address Layout
sections.content:
An NSAP address is built in layers. First comes the Authority and Format Identifier (AFI), which specifies the format and the authority in charge. Next is the Initial Domain Identifier (IDI), which pinpoints a particular subdomain under that authority. Together, AFI and IDI form the standardized IDP.

The DSP that follows is left to the administering authority. RFC 982 recommends dividing it into three fixed fields in a specific order. This structure allows different numbering authorities (X.121 for public data networks, telephone numbering for ISDN, organizational codes, and others) to use their own encoding while maintaining a predictable layout.
sections.eli5: Think of layers: international body → country → authority → organization → subnetwork → machine → service. Each layer is a separate field. The memo explains which fields are standardized and which the local authority controls.

sections.title: The Three DSP Fields
sections.content:
The DSP contains exactly three fields. First, subnetwork identification, a fixed-size field set by the administering authority to identify which subnetwork the address belongs to. A reserved value (hex FF in binary, 99999 in decimal) means the subnetwork is implicit. Second, subnetwork address, which typically holds the MAC address of a machine on that subnetwork, allowing variable length to accommodate different network types. Third, NSAP selector, a fixed-size field at the end identifying which service or process on the host should handle the packet—similar to a port number in IP.

The RFC specifies these field sizes for each common numbering authority. X.121 addresses, for instance, use 2-octet subnetwork IDs in binary format, but 5 decimal digits in decimal format. ISDN (E.164) and other authorities have their own sizes. Every authority gets both binary and decimal options.
sections.eli5: DSP is divided like an envelope: address block + building section + apartment number. The address block size depends on which postal authority you're in, but the pattern is always the same. This memo says: if you're X.121, use these sizes; if you're E.164, use those sizes.

sections.title: Guidance for Addressing Authorities
sections.content:
RFC 982 advises private and public address administration authorities to follow these guidelines when deploying networks with equipment from different suppliers. An authority can choose a numbering scheme (X.121 for public networks, ISO DCC for geography, ISO 6523-ICD for organizational codes) and then apply the corresponding DSP structure recommended in the memo.

This is a working draft and informational only, not a formal standard. The value is in providing a reference structure so that heterogeneous systems can be deployed without extensive reconfiguration. Following these guidelines ensures that an authority's address assignment decisions will work predictably across different vendors' equipment.
sections.eli5: If you're handing out addresses in your organization, pick a scheme (company ID, geography, whatever), then follow this memo's layout for the address. Everyone building systems for your network will then understand each other.
